property_summary: For any valid input, a successful call to transfer must return true; the mutant returns false, violating that post-condition.
The reference contract always reverts when the contract_address is zero, while the buggy version allows it and proceeds to make low-level calls.

The reference contract never allows a transfer where contract_address equals address(c). The bug allows it, causing the contract to call transferFrom on itself, which will succeed or fail depending on the contract's own logic, but notably allows a self-targeted transfer attempt that the reference correctly blocks.

For any admissible input where contract_address is not address(c), a call to transfer must not revert; the bug removes the check and allows self-calls which revert because the contract lacks a transferFrom function, breaking the no-revert guarantee.

The reference contract always invokes transferFrom with msg.sender as sender on the target token, while the mutant invokes transfer using the contract itself as sender, causing the external token to move tokens from contract C instead of msg.sender and breaking the invariant that each recipient's balance change reflects the value sent from msg.sender.

For any valid call to transfer, the external token contract's transferFrom must be called with msg.sender as the sender, not address(this); the reference always passes msg.sender, while the mutant incorrectly passes address(this).

For any non-empty arrays, a call to transfer always succeeds without reverting (because the reference enforces equal lengths before iterating, preventing out-of-bounds access and subsequent call failures), whereas the mutant allows mismatched lengths leading to an out-of-bounds array access that can cause a revert.

After calling transfer with non-empty tos and vs where tos.length <= vs.length, the reference C always returns true without reverting, while the mutant reverts when tos.length < vs.length due to out-of-bounds access on vs.

For any valid input arrays with tos.length > 0 and vs.length > 0, the reference C always completes the call without reverting if tos.length == vs.length, but the mutant can revert when tos.length != vs.length due to an out-of-bounds access on vs.

For any non-empty address and uint arrays where tos length <= vs length, the reference returns true without reverting, while the mutant reverts when tos length < vs length due to out-of-bounds access on vs.

The contract always processes exactly tos.length transfers when tos and vs have equal length; the mutant may process more or fewer, either accessing out-of-bounds elements or leaving some unreached when tos.length != vs.length and the loop bound is vs.length.

After a successful call to transfer with equal-length non-empty arrays, the number of transfers performed must equal tos.length; the mutant loops over vs.length, so when vs.length differs from tos.length the number of calls differs, violating the invariant that all legitimate tos entries are processed exactly once.

The transfer function must always revert when called; by supplying a contract_address that implements the required interface but reverts on the first low-level call, the reference succeeds in all iterations and returns true, whereas the mutant accesses out-of-bounds data, causing a revert.

After a successful call to transfer with equal-length arrays, the number of low-level calls executed must equal tos.length; the mutant loops over vs.length, so when the fuzzer supplies a malicious token that reverts only on the second call, the reference succeeds with both calls, but the mutant erroneously loops only once, skipping the reverting call, and thus does not revert.

For any valid equal-length arrays tos and vs, a successful transfer call must execute exactly tos.length low-level calls; the mutant loops over vs.length and when vs.length != tos.length (due to an attacker-controlled token that alters return behavior) it executes a different number of calls, violating the expected call count.

The function must succeed only when all external calls succeed; the mutant succeeds even when an external call fails, observable by checking that if any call fails the entire call reverts but the mutant returns true.
